name: Micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF)
short: Case reports: DRESS, a severe drug reaction (one with very high liver enzymes), after diosmin-hesperidin, form not stated. Report titled MPFF-induced slow heart rate. Trials: tolerated like placebo.
text: These data are for the micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF), taken by mouth, except where a sentence says its source concerns diosmin with hesperidin, or diosmin, without naming MPFF; a 2003 review describes MPFF as an oral drug consisting of 90% micronised diosmin and 10% flavonoids expressed as hesperidin. A 2025 report titled as a case of MPFF-induced bradycardia (slow heart rate) describes a significant fall in heart rate after 60 days of MPFF, from 88.8 to 79.3 beats per minute, with no significant change in blood pressure; the abstract does not say how many people were studied, and the authors call for further studies. The 2003 review reports that in clinical trials MPFF had a tolerability profile similar to placebo, the most frequent adverse events being gastrointestinal and autonomic. In a double-blind randomised trial in 162 people with acute haemorrhoids comparing two tablet strengths for 7 days, no serious adverse events occurred and 10 adverse events were considered treatment-related (6 and 4 in the two groups). In two randomised trials in chronic venous disease comparing once-daily formulations with twice-daily tablets for 8 weeks (309 and 302 patients randomised in one; 1,139 included in the other), tolerability was similar between formulations; neither had a placebo group. A 2022 meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (2,335 participants) after haemorrhoid surgery found no substantial effect on adverse reactions, and in a 63-patient randomised trial after stapled haemorrhoidopexy (30 given MPFF) there were no side effects from MPFF. In a report of 218 older patients with chronic venous disease whose 4-week treatment included MPFF and wound care, the safety assessment found no adverse reactions or worsening of other illnesses; the abstract does not say how many of the 218 took MPFF. In a pilot randomised trial of MPFF added to rivaroxaban in 60 people with deep vein thrombosis, the abstract gives no adverse-event or bleeding data. Two case reports describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), a severe skin and whole-body reaction, after diosmin with hesperidin; neither abstract says whether the product taken was MPFF. One of them gives a mortality rate of 3.8-10% for DRESS in general, not for these ingredients. In that report, a 34-year-old woman with atopy and venous insufficiency had itchy hives on the face and arms that progressed to a measles-like (morbilliform) rash, facial swelling, fever, swollen lymph nodes and scaling, with a very high liver enzyme (ALT 11,352 U/L); she had also used a systemic sunscreen product beforehand. She improved on three weeks of corticosteroids, but two months later the rash and raised liver enzymes returned, with a positive herpes simplex IgM test. The other report describes a 48-year-old man with DRESS resembling acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) after diosmin and hesperidin, and its authors call such reactions exceptionally rare. Interactions: in two open-label studies, each in 12 healthy men, diosmin taken daily for 10 days (the abstracts do not mention hesperidin or say whether the diosmin was micronised) raised blood levels of single doses of carbamazepine and of fexofenadine; these were pharmacokinetic studies, and the abstracts report no clinical outcomes. No other interaction data were found in the cited sources.
